extracted.intended_audience: U.S. employers, immigration attorneys, advocates, and policymakers concerned about H-1B implementation and compliance
extracted.subtask_description: Explains USCIS implementation of the presidential proclamation requiring a $100,000 payment tied to certain H-1B filings, detailing when the fee applies, exemptions, national-interest-exception criteria and procedures, and legal arguments challenging the proclamation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment timing and method requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If subject to the proclamation, payment must be made through pay.gov before a U.S. employer files an H-1B petition with USCIS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The U.S. employer/petitioner must submit either proof of payment or evidence that it received an exception or USCIS will deny the petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal filing exemption (pre-September 21 filings)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proclamation does not apply to petitions filed before 12:01 a.m. Eastern Time on September 21, 2025.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This means a noncitizen can be issued an H-1B visa, or be admitted to the United States in H-1B status—without the fee being collected—if the approved H-1B petition was filed before this deadline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existing valid H-1B visas exemption
rubrics_metrics.description: The proclamation does not apply to previously issued and currently valid H-1B visas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holders of already-issued, valid H-1B visas are not subject to the $100,000 payment under USCIS's explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee applies when beneficiary is abroad without a valid H-1B visa
rubrics_metrics.description: Fee payment or exception required if the beneficiary is outside the United States and does not have a valid H-1B visa at the time the H-1B petition is filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If this condition holds and no exception is shown, payment must be made before filing or petition will be denied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee applies when petition requests consular/port/preflight notification
rubrics_metrics.description: Fee payment or exception required if the beneficiary is in the United States but the H-1B petition requests consular, port of entry, or preflight inspection notification if USCIS approves the petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requesting such notifications with a petition filed on or after the effective date triggers the fee unless an exception applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: No fee for certain approved amendments/extensions/change-of-status filings (beneficiary in US at filing)
rubrics_metrics.description: No fee required to file an H-1B petition if USCIS approves an amended H-1B petition, or approves a request for extension of stay in H-1B status or a request for change of status from another nonimmigrant status to H-1B, provided the beneficiary is in the United States when the employer files the petition requesting the extension or change of status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USCIS's explanation emphasizes that beneficiary presence in the U.S. at filing is a condition for these no-fee scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: No fee for beneficiaries of previously approved petitions who later travel and seek visa/reentry
rubrics_metrics.description: No fee required for a beneficiary of an H-1B petition for which USCIS approved an amendment, extension of stay, or change of status who later travels abroad and applies for an H-1B visa based on that approved petition and/or seeks to reenter the United States on a valid H-1B visa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USCIS treats visa issuance/reentry based on a prior approved petition or valid visa as outside the proclamation's fee requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ineligibility or departure after filing can trigger fee
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS states that 'if a petition filed at or after 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight time on September 21, 2025, requests a change of status or amendment or extension of stay and USCIS determines that the noncitizen is ineligible for a change of status or an amendment or extension of stay (e.g., is not in a valid nonimmigrant visa status or if the [noncitizen] departs the United States prior to adjudication of a change of status request), the Proclamation will apply and the payment must be paid according to the instructions provided by USCIS.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates a potential trap: a petition that would otherwise avoid the fee may become subject to it if USCIS later finds the beneficiary ineligible or the beneficiary departs before adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: National interest exception (NIE) criteria (USCIS)
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS describes the NIE as requiring four criteria: (1) The noncitizen’s presence in the United States is in the national interest; (2) No 'American worker is available to fill the role.'; (3) The noncitizen does not pose a threat to the national security or welfare; (4) Requiring the U.S. employer/petitioner to pay the fee would 'significantly undermine U.S. interests.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USCIS characterizes the NIE as an 'extraordinarily rare circumstance' and limits relief to individual determinations rather than categorical grants by category or employer/industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: NIE procedural requirement: prior request and submission of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A U.S. employer must submit the exception request to a dedicated DHS email address before filing the H-1B petition, and USCIS requires that 'evidence of the exception' be submitted with an H-1B petition for which the fee otherwise would be due upon filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to submit prior request and documentary evidence with the petition will lead USCIS to deny the H-1B petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: USCIS denial for failure to provide payment or exception evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS will deny the H-1B petition if the employer/petitioner does not submit either proof of payment or evidence that it received an exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an enforcement mechanism—lack of documentation at filing is treated as a basis for denial rather than a notice-and-opportunity process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal grounds asserted to challenge the proclamation
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawsuits allege (a) the president lacks authority to create new H-1B program requirements (including fees) that Congress established; (b) the fee is not permitted by the president's authority to restrict entry and in one case is called an unlawful tax; and (c) agency implementation is unlawful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The complaints argue the proclamation's structure and requirements are inconsistent with its stated intent to restrict entry, and that tying the fee to petition filing (a USCIS action that does not determine entry) undermines the proclamation's asserted legal basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural critique: tying fee to petition filing inconsistent with entry restriction
rubrics_metrics.description: The proclamation ties the $100,000 payment to the filing of an H-1B petition even though USCIS approval of an H-1B petition is not enough for entry to the United States and USCIS does not decide who gets to enter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This inconsistency is presented as a vulnerability to legal attack and as evidence the proclamation addresses domestic program issues that existing law/regulation already can address, rather than a valid entry restriction.
